title: Student Engagement with GenAI’s Tutoring Feedback: A Mixed Methods Study
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students engage with immediate AI-generated tutoring feedback while solving programming tasks. The central question is not whether the feedback improves test scores, but how students perceive, interpret, and act on different feedback components during problem solving. The authors argue that understanding engagement is important because even high-quality feedback may be ineffective if learners do not read, trust, or use it.

To study this, the authors built the Tutor Kai learning environment for Python programming exercises and implemented four GenAI-generated feedback components: identifying problems, providing explanations/examples, giving a next-step hint, and offering a strategic approach. The system generated feedback with GPT-4.1 and presented it in a controlled online environment used in an introductory programming course. Data were collected through think-aloud protocols, eye-tracking, screen/audio recording, system logs, and a questionnaire.

The study was conducted with undergraduate students in an introductory programming course at a German university. Although 23 students participated, only 20 were included in the eye-tracking analysis due to technical issues. The tasks were six Python exercises aligned with course progression and students worked individually in a supervised lab-style session. The paper focuses on engagement patterns rather than comparing against a control condition.

The authors found that students frequently expressed understanding of the feedback, but a substantial minority reported needing more information, disagreed with the feedback, or judged it unhelpful. Students often responded to unclear or irrelevant feedback by collecting another feedback component rather than changing their code immediately. When students indicated understanding, code improvements were much more likely. Overall, the study suggests that GenAI tutoring feedback can support learning, but learners need sufficient specificity and opportunities for follow-up to make effective use of it.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative mixed-methods study using think-aloud protocols, eye-tracking, screen recordings, and inductive/deductive coding rather than an experimental causal design. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically detailed, but it does not meet RCT or quasi-experimental credibility criteria for higher tiers.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows useful but context-specific evidence of how students engage with GenAI feedback, with descriptive rates such as 82.0% improvement after a feedback request and 55.8% component collection. Because it is qualitative, small-scale, and focused on engagement rather than a causal learning effect, the broader impact is informative but modest/unclear.

interventions.use_case: GenAI-generated immediate tutoring feedback for introductory Python programming tasks, delivered as four selectable feedback components (problem identification, explanations/examples, next-step hint, strategic approach).

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative mixed-methods study with n=20 undergraduate programming students found that feedback engagement was often supportive but not uniformly so. Students verbally expressed understanding in 45.5% of coded thoughts, but 21.6% indicated missing information and 18.7% expressed disagreement; additionally, 14.3% of thoughts were explicit judgments of helpfulness. Directly observable engagement showed that students collected 55.8% of 688 generated feedback components and read 380 of 384 collected components, suggesting selective but active engagement.
finding.measure: Think-aloud coding of feedback-related thoughts; feedback collection and reading rates from logs and eye-tracking

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily examines feedback literacy, self-regulation, and metacognitive engagement with AI-generated feedback. In 82.0% of 172 GenAI feedback requests, at least one collected and read component led to an improvement, and 69.5% of cases with thoughts indicating disagreement or missing information were followed by no immediate action rather than an incorrect code change. However, setbacks and mixed outcomes still occurred, showing that understanding feedback did not always translate into correct implementation.
finding.measure: Think-aloud categories, immediate code-action coding (improvement, setback, both, no action), and feedback collection behavior
